newsitem.title: INDIA: Allies say India coalition may not last full term.
newsitem.headline: Allies say India coalition may not last full term.

text.p: Key partners of Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's United Front alliance said on Wednesday they did not see the seven-month old coalition government lasting its five-year term.

Deve Gowda's first test of the new year will come later this week when the Congress elects a new leader to head the party in parliament. The Congress has 137 lawmakers in the 545-seat lower house of the parliament and provides a make-or-break support to the minority government.

The prime minister's partners cited rumblings within the disparate coalition over economic reforms and questions about the commitment by the Congress party to support Deve Gowda indefinitely as reasons for their assessment.

The Congress is divided over its support to the government. The rift widened in September when new Congress president Sitaram Kesri took over the party's leadership from former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao.
Kesri, making a bid for the Congress Parliamentary Party's (CPP) leadership, is regarded as a threat to the United Front government.

A Congress spokesman said a meeting of the party's top leaders decided on Wednesday to set up a three-member committee to evolve a consensus on the CPP leader this week, but the move was challenged by at least one leader.
"Our view from day one was that the term of the government will be short-lived, though no one knows how short-lived," one deputy of Deve Gowda's Janata Dal party told Reuters.

"It cannot. That we are clear about," Jyoti Basu, the communist chief minister of the West Bengal state, told the Asian Age newspaper. He was responding to a question if the alliance government could last its term.

"I told Deve Gowda, why should you bother about that (the full term)," Basu said in the interview published on Wednesday, adding that his Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPI-M) was urging the alliance to look after the poor.
"Later on, if you are thrown out, you are thrown out. If we are still together then, then it is a sort of election manifesto for you," Basu said.

Basu was named the alliance candidate for the prime minister's job, but the CPI-M central committee, which does not want an active role in a federal government, opposed the move and paved the way for Deve Gowda.
"It was a political blunder. It is a historic blunder," Basu said of the central committee's decision to keep out of the government.
He said Deve Gowda, as a pro-reform politician in a socialist Janata Dal party, was not much different from the Congress party leadership which started India's economic reforms in 1991.
"In economic thinking and all that I don't think he differs all that much," Basu said.
Kesari's two rivals for the CPP job -- former ministers Rajesh Pilot and Sharad Pawar -- want Congress to continue support to Deve Gowda, with the possibility of eventually joining the government.
The United Front alliance has 190 deputies in the lower house.
Kesri, a shrewd tactician, wants to split the alliance and head a government under Congress leadership, politicians say.
If he succeeds in getting the CPP job, Kesri's hands would be strengthened to carry out that plan, his aides say.
